Council of Orange (AD 529)
KOWN-sil uv OR-inj
noun (church council)
Named for the town of Orange (Latin Arausio) in southern Gaul, where the synod met in 529; council from Latin concilium, an assembly.

📖 Biblical Definition

The Council of Orange, convened in AD 529 under the presidency of Caesarius of Arles, is one of the brightest patristic witnesses to the doctrines of grace and a true forerunner of the Reformed faith. It met to condemn semi-Pelagianism, the cunning compromise that granted man a corrupted will yet left him able to take the first step toward God—to begin to believe—before grace was given. Orange swept this away. It decreed that not only the increase but the very beginning of faith and the longing to believe are the work of the Holy Spirit within us, that grace is not given according to our merits but goes before all our good willing and working. It confessed that by Adam's sin the whole man, body and soul, was changed for the worse, and that no one of himself has anything but lying and sin. Here is the substance of total depravity and the priority of grace, the very marrow our standards would later confess in fuller form. The council affirmed too that God predestines men to good, and it anathematized the dreadful error that any are predestined to evil by divine power—a careful witness the Reformed gladly own, for our doctrine of reprobation is a passing by, not a positive authoring of sin. Orange shows that monergism is no Genevan novelty but the ancient faith.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The synod of AD 529 that condemned semi-Pelagianism and affirmed the priority of grace and predestination unto good, anticipating Reformed soteriology.

expand to see more

COUNCIL OF ORANGE, noun [from Orange, Latin Arausio, in Gaul.] A synod held in 529 under Caesarius of Arles to settle the controversy over grace and free will.

Condemned semi-Pelagianism, the teaching that man begins to believe before grace.

Affirmed that the very beginning of faith is the gift of the Holy Spirit.

Confessed the predestination of men unto good and anathematized predestination unto evil.

“For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure.” Philippians 2:13.

Php 2:13 — "For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure."

Joh 6:44 — "No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day."

Eph 2:1 — "And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins;"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

An ancient council whose teaching is sound; the danger is a revived semi-Pelagianism that flatters the natural will.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the priority of grace over the will. Orange condemned semi-Pelagianism—the notion that the sinner takes the first step toward God before grace moves him—and the same error lives on wherever men preach that God helps those who help themselves, or that conversion begins with the unaided human decision.

Modern revivalism and free-will religion repeat the very compromise Orange anathematized, making grace a response to man's initiative rather than its cause. But Scripture asks, “what hast thou that thou didst not receive?” and answers that God works in us both to will and to do. To recover Orange is to recover monergism: the dead are quickened, the unwilling are made willing, and from first to last salvation is of the Lord.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The name fixes the council to a Gallic town; council springs from the Latin for an assembly called together.

expand to see more

Orange — from Latin Arausio, a town in southern Gaul.

concilium — Latin, an assembly summoned for counsel.

Convened in 529 under Caesarius, bishop of Arles.

Drew heavily on Augustine against the heirs of Pelagius.

A patristic seedbed of the later Reformed doctrine of grace.

Usage

"Long before Geneva, the Council of Orange confessed that the beginning of faith is the gift of the Spirit."

"We answered the free-will preacher from the Council of Orange, which condemned his semi-Pelagianism by name."

"The Council of Orange shows that sovereign grace is the ancient faith, not a sixteenth-century invention."
